entries.c6f7b470c5fa734780932fd0afb429f1e5883ae5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9360"/><div sID="gen16148" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9360"/><hi type="bold">11. not comforted--</hi>by anyone; none gave her help or comfort.<div eID="gen16148" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16149" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">lay ... with fair colours--</hi>rather, "lay ... in cement of vermilion" [Lowth]. The Hebrew for "fair colors" means stibium, the paint with which Eastern women painted their eyelids and eyelashes (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.9.30">2Ki 9:30</reference>). The very cement shall be of the most beautiful color (<reference osisRef="Rev.21.18-Rev.21.21">Re 21:18-21</reference>). <div eID="gen16149" type="x-p"/>
entries.f2c63735db6a6ac8c6ce5b1a7b901d9cdd0f82e9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9361"/><div sID="gen16150" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9361"/><hi type="bold">12. windows--</hi>rather, "battlements"; literally, "suns"; applied to battlements from their radiated appearance.<div eID="gen16150" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16151" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">agates--</hi>rather, "rubies."<div eID="gen16151" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16152" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">carbuncles--</hi>literally, "sparkling gems"; the carbuncle when held to the sun becomes like a burning coal.<div eID="gen16152" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16153" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">all thy borders--</hi>rather, "thy whole circuit," consisting of precious stones. The glory of the Church on earth, when the Hebrew Church, according to the original design, shall be the metropolis of Christendom. <div eID="gen16153" type="x-p"/>
entries.28effb07f11d10694cabeb37ffebab258e4a2e15: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9362"/><div sID="gen16154" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9362"/>13. Quoted by the Saviour (<reference osisRef="John.6.45">Joh 6:45</reference>), to prove that in order to come to Him, men must be "drawn" by the Father. So <reference osisRef="Jer.31.34">Jr 31:34</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.4.2">Mi 4:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.10">1Co 2:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.8.10">He 8:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.10.16">10:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="1John.2.20">1Jo 2:20</reference>.<div eID="gen16154" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16155" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">great ... peace--</hi>generally (<reference osisRef="Ps.119.165">Psa 119:165</reference>). Specially referring to the peaceful prosperity which shall prevail under Messiah in the latter days (<reference osisRef="Isa.2.4">Is 2:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.9.6">9:6</reference>). <div eID="gen16155" type="x-p"/>
entries.45d70375504b8e59ec615df2775a1972d30827b2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9363"/><div sID="gen16156" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9363"/><hi type="bold">14. righteousness--</hi>the characteristic of the reign of Messiah (<reference osisRef="Isa.11.4">Is 11:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.11.5">5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.72.2">Psa 72:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.72.4">4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.19.11">Re 19:11</reference>).<div eID="gen16156" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16157" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">far from oppression, &c.--</hi>far from suffering oppression; "for thou shall have nothing to fear." <div eID="gen16157" type="x-p"/>
entries.46f93b9324e5203c5d7fdfc399884994f63f86b6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9364"/><div sID="gen16158" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9364"/><hi type="bold">15. gather together, &c.--</hi>that is, If it should happen that enemies "gather together" against thee (<reference osisRef="Ps.2.2">Psa 2:2</reference>), they will not have been sent by Me (compare <reference osisRef="Hos.8.4">Ho 8:4</reference>) as instruments of My wrath (nay, it will be with My disapproval); for "whosoever shall gather together," &c. (<reference osisRef="Ps.59.3">Psa 59:3</reference>).<div eID="gen16158" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16159" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fall for thy sake--</hi>rather, "shall come over to thy side" [Lowth]. Literally, "fall to thee" (<reference osisRef="Jer.21.9">Jr 21:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.39.9">39:9</reference>). To be fully fulfilled to Jerusalem hereafter (<reference osisRef="Zech.14.16">Zec 14:16</reference>). <div eID="gen16159" type="x-p"/>
entries.61b9ea3780cb00a270f5c591679d5dcbc8c1ed23: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9365"/><div sID="gen16160" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9365"/>16. The workman that forms "weapons against thee" (<reference osisRef="Isa.54.17">Is 54:17</reference>) is wholly in My power, therefore thou needest not fear, having Me on thy side.<div eID="gen16160" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16161" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for his work--</hi>rather, "by his labor [Horsley]. "According to the exigencies of his work" [Maurer].<div eID="gen16161" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16162" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">waster to destroy--</hi>(Is 10:5-7; 37:26, 27; <reference osisRef="Isa.45.1-Isa.45.6">45:1-6</reference>). Desolating conquerors who use the "instruments" framed by "the smith." The repetition of the "I" implies, however, something in the latter half of the verse contrasted with the former understand it, therefore, thus: "I have in My power both him who frames arms and him who destroys them (arms)" [Rosenmuller]. <div eID="gen16162" type="x-p"/>
entries.aa2c226faadd24d3d4f82887fad9bc73696036e7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9366"/><div sID="gen16163" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9366"/><hi type="bold">17. tongue ... condemn--</hi>image from a court of justice. Those who desire to "condemn" thee thou shalt "condemn" (<reference osisRef="Exod.11.7">Ex 11:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.10.21">Jos 10:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.64.8">Psa 64:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.8.1">Ro 8:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.8.33">33</reference>).<div eID="gen16163" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16164" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">righteousness ... of me--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.45.24">Is 45:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.46.13">46:13</reference>). Rather, "(this is) their justification from Me." Their enemies would "condemn" them, but I justify and vindicate them, and so they condemn their enemies. <chapter eID="Isa.54"/>

entries.4d78d0d59571b33dbbf1be9ea42c81adeb35bcc9: <div eID="gen28683" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen28684" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen28685" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen28685" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen28684" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen28686" type="x-p"/> Some suppose this chapter to have been addressed to the Gentiles; some, to the Jewish Church; and some, to the Christian, in its first stage. On comparing the different parts of it, particularly the seventh and eighth verses, with the remainder, the most obvious import of the prophecy will be that which refers it to the future conversion of the Jews, and to the increase and prosperity of that nation, when reconciled to God after their long rejection, when their glory and security will far surpass what they were formerly in their most favored state, vv. 1-17. <div eID="gen28686" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28687" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen28687" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28688" type="x-p"/> Sing, O barren, thou that didst not bear "Shout for joy, O thou barren, that didst not bear" - The Church of God under the Old Testament, confined within the narrow bounds of the Jewish nation, and still more so in respect of the very small number of true believers, and which sometimes seemed to be deserted of God her husband, is the barren woman, that did not bear, and was desolate. She is exhorted to rejoice, and to express her joy in the strongest manner, on the reconciliation of her husband, (see <reference osisRef="Isa.54.6">Isa 54:6</reference>), and on the accession of the Gentiles to her family. The converted Gentiles are all along considered by the prophet as a new accession of adopted children, admitted into the original Church of God, and united with it. See <reference osisRef="Isa.49.20">Isa 49:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.49.21">Isa 49:21</reference>.
entries.e08d05aa0518ca0db4af7ae561560d99c48c6f50: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen28688" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28689" type="x-p"/> For thou shalt forget the shame of thy youth - That is, "The bondage of Egypt: widowhood, the captivity of Babylon." - Secker.
entries.3aa44b84139d396cce0f3806ebffb296b1e53b3d: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen28689" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28690" type="x-p"/> For a small moment "In a little anger" - So the Chaldee and Syriac, either reading רגז regaz, for רגע rega; or understanding the latter word as meaning the same with the former, which they both make use of. See <reference osisRef="Psa.30.5">Psa 30:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Psa.35.20">Psa 35:20</reference>, in the Septuagint, where they render רגע rega by οργη, anger.
entries.5a76d891dfff486043f4ac0a4461a2806ad35046: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen28690" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28691" type="x-p"/> I hid my face from thee for a moment - The word רגע rega is omitted by the Septuagint, Syriac, and two MSS. of Kennicott's, and two of De Rossi's. It seems to embarrass rather than to help the sentence. Forte reponi debet pro שצף shetseph, quod potest a קצף ketseph errore scribae originem duxisse. "Perhaps it ought to be substituted for שצף shetseph, an error probably made by some scribe from its similarity to קצף ketseph." - Secker <div eID="gen28691" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28692" type="x-p"/> Thy Redeemer - גאלך goalech: but for this word three of De Rossi's MSS. have מרחמך merachamech, thy commiserator.
entries.f9f8413fcfe84d41f5e863f177a7dc1b1cfd0705: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen28692" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28693" type="x-p"/> For this is as the waters of Noah unto me "The same will I do now, as in the days of Noah" - כימי kimey, in one word, in a MS., and some editions; and so the Syriac, Chaldee, Vulgate, Symmachus, Theodotion, Abarbanel, Sal. ben Melec, and Kimchi acknowledge that their copies vary in this place. <div eID="gen28693" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28694" type="x-p"/> It is certain that these two words כי מי ki mey, were written formerly as one. Taken as two כי מי ki mey, they signify for as the waters - when as one, כימי kimey, they signify as the days. This latter reading is found in about four of Kennicott's and De Rossi's MSS. In one of my own it appears to have been intended as one word: but he who added the points, which are by a much later hand than the MS. itself, has pointed the letters so as to make the two words which are commonly found in the text. For the waters, Symmachus, Theodotion, the Syriac, Vulgate, and Arabic have days. The former seems to make the best sense; and the ancient Versions, except the Septuagint, support it.
entries.85a128394289778edd92aacde9462df4f4a7b176: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen28694" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28695" type="x-p"/> Behold, I will lay thy stones "Behold, I lay thy stones" - These seem to be general images to express beauty, magnificence, purity, strength, and solidity, agreeably to the ideas of the eastern nations; and to have never been intended to be strictly scrutinized, or minutely and particularly explained, as if they had each of them some precise, moral, or spiritual meaning. Tobit, in his prophecy of the final restoration of Israel, describes the New Jerusalem in the same oriental manner: "For Jerusalem shall be built up with sapphires, and emeralds, and precious stones; thy walls, and towers, and battlements, with pure gold. And the streets of Jerusalem shall be paved with beryl, and carbuncle, and stones of ophir." Tob. 13:16, 17. Compare also <reference osisRef="Rev.21.18-Rev.21.21">Rev 21:18-21</reference>.
entries.2bb0814ad81cb54d23116c339b729488578691f7: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen28695" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28696" type="x-p"/> Shall fall for thy sake "Shall come over to thy side" - For יפול yippol, twenty-eight MSS. (eight ancient) have יפל yipal, in its more common form. For the meaning of the word in this place, see <reference osisRef="Jer.37.13">Jer 37:13</reference>.  <chapter eID="Isa.54"/> <div eID="gen28696" type="x-p"/>

entries.5e936d8508cb4dfd8330851cf74120c062d35a81: <reference osisRef="Isa.54.1">Isa 54:1</reference> <div eID="gen13532" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13533" type="x-p"/> After the “Servant of God” has expiated the sin of His people by the sacrifice of Himself, and Israel has acknowledged its fault in connection with the rejected One, and entered into the possession and enjoyment of the salvation procured by Him, the glory of the church, which has thus become a partaker of salvation through repentance and faith, is quite ready to burst forth. Hence the prophet can now exclaim, <reference osisRef="Isa.54.1">Isa 54:1</reference> : <hi type="italic">“Exult, O barren one, thou that didst not bear; break forth into exulting, and cry aloud, thou that didst not travail with child: for there are more children of the solitary one than children of the married wife, saith Jehovah.”</hi> The words are addressed to Jerusalem, which was a counterpart of Sarah in her barrenness at first, and her fruitfulness afterwards (<reference osisRef="Isa.41.1-Isa.41.3">Isa 41:1-3</reference>). She is not תלד לא עקרה (<reference osisRef="Job.24.21">Job 24:21</reference>), but ילדה לא עקרה (Jdg 13:2); not indeed that she had never had any children, but during her captivity and exile she had been robbed of her children, and as a holy city had given birth to no more (<reference osisRef="Isa.49.21">Isa 49:21</reference>). She was <hi type="italic">shōmēmâh</hi>, rendered <hi type="italic">solitary</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Sam.13.20">2Sa 13:20</reference>; the allusion is to her depopulation as a city), whereas formerly she was בּעוּלה, i.e., enjoyed the fellowship of Jehovah her husband (<hi type="italic">ba‛al</hi>). But this condition would not last (for Jehovah had not given her a divorce): she was therefore to exult and shout, since the number of children which she would now have, as one desolate and solitary, would be greater than the number of those which she had as a married wife.
entries.3ff09921bd5c6930bf9db93177e6e34a4c0d5f08: <reference osisRef="Isa.54.2">Isa 54:2</reference> <div eID="gen13533" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13534" type="x-p"/> With this prospect before her, even her dwelling-place would need enlarging. <hi type="italic">“Enlarge the space of thy tent, and let them stretch out the curtains of thy habitations; forbid not! lengthen thy cords, and fasten thy plugs.”</hi> She is to widen out the space inside her tent, and they (יטּוּ has no definite subject, which is often the case where some subordinate servant is to be thought of) are to spread out far and wide the coverings of the framework of her dwelling, which is called <hi type="italic">mishkenōth</hi> (in the plural) on account of its roominess and magnificence: she is not to forbid it, thinking in her weakness of faith, “It is good enough as it is; it would be too large.” The cords which hold up the walls, she is to lengthen; and the plugs, to which the cords are fastened, she is to ram fast into the earth: the former because the tent (i.e., the holy city, <reference osisRef="Jer.31.38-Jer.31.40">Jer 31:38-40</reference>, and the dwelling-place of the church generally, <reference osisRef="Isa.26.15">Isa 26:15</reference>) has to receive a large number of inhabitants; the latter because it will not be broken up so soon again (<reference osisRef="Isa.33.20">Isa 33:20</reference>).
entries.ba48335b3e1dcdd6237e00a7cd69d9045595ea08: <reference osisRef="Isa.54.3">Isa 54:3</reference> <div eID="gen13534" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13535" type="x-p"/> The reason why the tent is to be so large and strong is given in <reference osisRef="Isa.54.3">Isa 54:3</reference> : <hi type="italic">“For thou wilt break forth on the right and on the left; and thy seed will take possession of nations, and they will people desolate cities.”</hi> “On the right and on the left” is equivalent to “on the south and north” (<reference osisRef="Ps.89.13">Psa 89:13</reference>, the speaker being supposed to have his face turned towards the east: compare the Sanscrit <hi type="italic">apân</hi>, situated at the back, i.e., towards the west). We must supply both west and east, since the promises contained in such passages as <reference osisRef="Gen.15.18-Gen.15.21">Gen 15:18-21</reference> remained unfulfilled even in the age of David and Solomon. Jerusalem will now spread out, and break through all her former bounds (<hi type="italic">pârats</hi> is used in the same sense in <reference osisRef="Gen.28.14">Gen 28:14</reference>); and her seed (i.e., the seed acquired by the Servant of Jehovah, the dead yet eternally living One, the σπέρμα, whose σπέρμα He Himself is) will take possession of nations (<hi type="italic">yârash</hi>, <hi type="italic">yârēsh</hi>, <hi type="italic">capessere</hi>, <hi type="italic">occupare</hi>; more especially κληρονομεῖν, syn. <hi type="italic">nâchal</hi>); and they (i.e., the children born to her) will people desolate cities (<hi type="italic">hōshı̄bh</hi>, the causative of <hi type="italic">yâshabh</hi>, to be inhabited, <reference osisRef="Isa.14.20">Isa 14:20</reference>). Thus will the promise be fulfilled, that “the meek shall inherit the earth,” - a promise not confined to the Preacher on the mount, but found also in <reference osisRef="Ps.37.9-Ps.37.11">Psa 37:9-11</reference>, and uttered by our own prophet in <reference osisRef="Isa.60.21">Isa 60:21</reference>; Isa 65:9.
entries.6f21525717c11c96f3354cdc2e814fc591d4d9d1: <reference osisRef="Isa.54.4">Isa 54:4</reference> <div eID="gen13535" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13536" type="x-p"/> The encouraging promise is continued in <reference osisRef="Isa.54.4">Isa 54:4</reference> : <hi type="italic">“Fear not, for thou wilt not be put to shame; and bid defiance to reproach, for thou wilt not blush: no, thou wilt forget the shame of thy youth, and wilt no more remember the reproach of thy widowhood.”</hi> Now that redemption was before the door, Israel was not to fear any more, or to be overcome (as the <hi type="italic">niphal nikhlam</hi> implies) by a felling of the shame consequent upon her state of punishment, or so to behave herself as to leave no room for hope. For a state of things was about to commence, in which she would have no need to be ashamed (on <hi type="italic">bōsh</hi> and <hi type="italic">châphēr</hi> or <hi type="italic">hechpı̄r</hi>), but which, on the contrary (כּי, <hi type="italic">imo</hi>, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.10.7">Isa 10:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.55.9">Isa 55:9</reference>), would be so glorious that she would forget the shame of her youth, i.e., of the Egyptian bondage, in which the national community of Israel was still but like a virgin (<hi type="italic">‛almâh</hi>), who entered into a betrothal when redeemed by Jehovah, and became His youthful wife through a covenant of love (<hi type="italic">ehe</hi> = <hi type="italic">berı̄th</hi>) when the law was given at Sinai (<reference osisRef="Jer.2.2">Jer 2:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.60">Eze 16:60</reference>); so glorious indeed, that she would never again remember the shame of her widowhood, i.e., of the Babylonian captivity, in which she, the wife whom Jehovah had taken to Himself, was like a widow whose husband had died.
entries.d7facfbc79dd5df2232f6cde23b1caebd5b23f2b: <reference osisRef="Isa.54.5">Isa 54:5</reference> <div eID="gen13536" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13537" type="x-p"/> It was no real widowhood, however, but only an apparent one (<reference osisRef="Jer.51.5">Jer 51:5</reference>), for the husband of Jerusalem was living still, <hi type="italic">“For thy husband is thy Creator; Jehovah of hosts is His name; and thy Redeemer the Holy One of Israel; God of the whole earth is He called.”</hi> The plurals בעליך and עשׂיך (see at <reference osisRef="Isa.22.11">Isa 22:11</reference>) are to be explained from the plural <hi type="italic">'Elōhı̄m</hi>, which is connected with plural attributes in <reference osisRef="Josh.24.19">Jos 24:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.26">1Sa 17:26</reference>, Ps. 58:12 (compare מרימיו in <reference osisRef="Isa.10.15">Isa 10:15</reference>), and with plural predicates in <reference osisRef="Gen.20.13">Gen 20:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.35.7">Gen 35:7</reference>, and 2Sa 7:23. By such expressions as these, which represent all the plurality of the divine nature as inherent in the One, the religion of revelation, both Israelitish and Christian, exhibits itself as embodying all that is true in polytheism. He who has entered into the relation of husband to Jerusalem (בעליך, not בעליך, <reference osisRef="Isa.1.3">Isa 1:3</reference>) is the very same through whom she first came into existence, the God whose bidding the heavenly hosts obey; and the Redeemer of Jerusalem, the Holy One of Israel, is called the God of the whole earth, and therefore has both the power and the means to help her, as prompted by the relation of love which exists between them.
entries.326eea12207ba211d6d5522125dcd69c25b52d24: <reference osisRef="Isa.54.6">Isa 54:6</reference> <div eID="gen13537" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13538" type="x-p"/> And this relation He now renews. <hi type="italic">“For Jehovah calleth thee as a wife forsaken and burdened with sorrow, and as a wife of youth, when once she is despised, saith thy God.”</hi> The verb קרא, which is the one commonly used in these prophecies to denote the call of grace, on the ground of the election of grace, is used here to signify the call into that relation, which did indeed exist before, but had apparently been dissolved. קראך is used here out of pause (cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.60.9">Isa 60:9</reference>); it stands, however, quite irregularly for the form in <hi type="italic">ēkh</hi>, which is the one commonly employed (Jdg 4:20; <reference osisRef="Ezek.27.26">Eze 27:26</reference>). “And as a wife:” ואשׁת is equivalent to וּכאשׁת. The hypothetical תמּאס כּי belongs to the figure. Jehovah calls His church back to Himself, as a husband takes back the wife he loved in his youth, even though he may once have been angry with her. It is with intention that the word נמאסה is not used. The future (imperfect) indicates what partially happens, but does not become an accomplished or completed fact: He is displeased with her, but He has not cherished aversion or hatred towards her.
entries.569e06e6dc17ed2840e722af77ed0e195fe4ebdc: <reference osisRef="Isa.54.7-Isa.54.8">Isa 54:7-8</reference> <div eID="gen13538" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13539" type="x-p"/> Thus does Jehovah’s displeasure towards Jerusalem pass quickly away; and all the more intense is the manifestation of love which follows His merely momentary anger. <hi type="italic">“For a small moment have I forsaken thee, and with great mercy will I gather thee. In an effusion of anger I hid my face from thee for a moment, and with everlasting grace I have compassion upon thee, saith Jehovah thy Redeemer.”</hi> “For a small moment” carries us to the time of the captivity, which was a small moment in comparison with the duration of the tender and merciful love, with which Jehovah once more received the church into His fellowship in the person of its members. רגע in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Isa.54.8">Isa 54:8</reference></hi> is not an adverb, meaning momentarily, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.47.9">Isa 47:9</reference>, but an accusative of duration, signifying a single moment long. <hi type="italic">Ketseph</hi> signifies wrath regarded as an outburst (<hi type="italic">fragor</hi>), like the violence of a storm or a clap of thunder; <hi type="italic">shetseph</hi>, which rhymes with it, is explained by A. Schultens, after the Arabic, as signifying <hi type="italic">durum et asperum esse</hi>: and hence the rendering adopted by Hitzig, “in hard harshness.” But this yields no antithesis to “everlasting kindness,” which requires that <hi type="italic">shetseph</hi> should be rendered in some way that expresses the idea of something transitory or of short duration. The earlier translators felt this, when like the lxx for example, they adopted the rendering ἐν θυμῷ μικρῷ, and others of a similar kind; and Ibn Labrât, in his writing against Menahem b. Zerûk, who gives <hi type="italic">chŏrı̄</hi>, burning heat, as a gloss to <hi type="italic">shetseph</hi>, explains it by מעט (as Kimchi and others did afterwards). But, as Jakob Tam correctly observes, “this makes the sense purely tautological.” In all probability, <hi type="italic">shâtsaph</hi> is a form allied to <hi type="italic">shâtaph</hi>, as <hi type="italic">nâshabh</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.40.7">Isa 40:7</reference>) is to <hi type="italic">nâshaph</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.40.24">Isa 40:24</reference>), and <hi type="italic">qâmat</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.16.8">Job 16:8</reference>) to <hi type="italic">qâmats</hi>, which stand in the same relation to one another, so far as the sense is concerned, as bubbling over to flowing over: so that the proper rendering would not be “in the overflowing of glowing heat,” as Umbreit thinks, which would require קצף בּשׁטף (<reference osisRef="Prov.27.4">Pro 27:4</reference>), but in the gushing up of displeasure, the overflowing of indignation (Meier). The <hi type="italic">ketseph</hi> is only a <hi type="italic">shetseph</hi>, a vanishing moment (Jer. <hi type="italic">in momento indignationis</hi>), when compared with the true feeling of Jehovah towards Jerusalem, which is <hi type="italic">chesed</hi> <hi type="italic">‛ōlâm</hi>, everlasting kindness.
entries.fb82e943f0c4d08d8fda6d3843b9b8421402a4a1: <reference osisRef="Isa.54.9">Isa 54:9</reference> <div eID="gen13539" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13540" type="x-p"/> The ground of this “everlasting kindness” is given in <reference osisRef="Isa.54.9">Isa 54:9</reference> : <hi type="italic">“For it is now as at the waters of Noah, when I swore that the waters of Noah should not overflow the earth any more; so have I sworn not to be wroth with thee, and not to threaten thee.”</hi> The commencement of this v. has been a fluctuating one from the earliest times. The Sept. reading is ממּי; that of the Targ., S., Jerome, Syriac, and Saad., כּימי; and even the Codd. read sometimes כּי־מי, sometimes כּימי (compare <reference osisRef="Matt.24.37">Mat 24:37</reference>, ὥσπερ αἱ ἡμέραι τοῦ Νῶε οὕτως κ.τ.λ - a passage which appears to derive its shape from the one before us, with the reading כימי, and which is expounded in <reference osisRef="Luke.17.26">Luk 17:26</reference>). If we read כימי, the word זאת must refer to the present, as the turning-point between wrath and mercy; but if we read כי־מי, זאת denotes the pouring out of wrath in connection with the captivity. Both readings are admissible; and as even the Septuagint, with its ἀπὸ τοῦ ὕδατος (from the water), gives an indirect support to the reading כּימי as one word, this may probably merit the preference, as the one best sustained. אשׁר is <hi type="italic">ubi</hi>, <hi type="italic">quum</hi>, as in Num 20:13; <reference osisRef="Ps.95.9">Psa 95:9</reference>, etc., although it might also be taken as the correlate of the <hi type="italic">kēn</hi> which follows, as in <reference osisRef="Jer.33.22">Jer 33:22</reference> (cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.48.8">Isa 48:8</reference>); and in accordance with the accents, we prefer the former. The present turning-point resembles, in Jehovah’s esteem, the days of Noah - those days in which He swore that a flood should not any more come upon the earth (<hi type="italic">min</hi> as in <reference osisRef="Isa.5.6">Isa 5:6</reference> and many other passages): for so does He now confirm with an oath His fixed purpose that no such judgment of wrath as that which has just been endured shall ever fall upon Jerusalem again (גּער denotes threatening with a judicial word, which passes at once into effect, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.51.20">Isa 51:20</reference>). Hendewerk has the following quibbling remark here: “What the comparison with the flood is worth, we may gather from the alter history, which shows how soon the new Jerusalem and the renovated state succumbed to the judicial wrath of God again.” To this we reply: (1.) That the prophecy refers to the converted Israel of the last days, whose Jerusalem will never be destroyed again. These last days appear to the prophet, according to the general character of all prophecy, as though linked on to the close of the captivity. For throughout all prophecy, along with the far-sightedness imparted by the Spirit, there was also a short-sightedness which the Spirit did not remove; that is to say, the directly divine element of <hi type="italic">insight</hi> into the future was associated with a human element of <hi type="italic">hope</hi>, which was nevertheless also indirectly divine, inasmuch as it subserved the divine plan of salvation; and this hope brought, as it were, the far distant future into the closest proximity with the troubled present. If, the, we keep this in mind, we shall see that it was quite in order for the prophet to behold the final future on the very edge of the present, and not to see the long and undulating way between. (2.) The Israel which has been plunged by the Romans into the present exile of a thousand years is that part of the nation (<reference osisRef="Rom.11.25">Rom 11:25</reference>), which has thrust away the eternal mercy and the unchangeable covenant of peace; but this rejection has simply postponed, and not prevented, the full realization of the salvation promised to Israel as a people. The <hi type="italic">covenant</hi> still exists, primarily indeed as an offer on the part of Jehovah, so that it rests with Israel whether it shall continued one-sided or not; but all that is wanted on the part of Israel is faith, to enable it to exchange the shifting soil of its present exile for the rocky foundation of that covenant of peace which has encircled the ages since the captivity (see Hag 2:9), as the covenant with Noah encircled those after the flood with the covenant sign of the rainbow in the cloud.
entries.98efeb2b28919fd6da86b9e0b3f3af41c0d8052e: <reference osisRef="Isa.54.10">Isa 54:10</reference> <hi type="italic">“For the mountains may depart, and the hills may shake; my grace will not depart from thee, and my covenant of peace will not shake, saith Jehovah who hath compassion on thee.”</hi> Jehovah’s grace and covenant of peace (cf., Num 25:12) stand as firm as the mountains of God (<reference osisRef="Ps.36.7">Psa 36:7</reference>), without departing from Jerusalem (מאתּך instead of the usual מאתּך) and without shaking; and they will be fulfilled. This fulfilment will not take place either by force or by enchantment; but the church which is to be glorified must pass through sufferings, until it has attained the form which answers to the glory promised to it on oath. And this will also take place; for the old Jerusalem will come forth as a new one out of the furnace of affliction.
entries.165de343d914d7bf01d0c633143200884ef41538: <reference osisRef="Isa.54.11-Isa.54.12">Isa 54:11-12</reference> <hi type="italic">“O thou afflicted, tossed with tempest, not comforted, behold, I lay thy stones in stibium, and lay thy foundations with sapphires; and make thy minarets of ruby, and thy gates into carbuncles, and all thy boundary into jewels.”</hi> At the present time the church, of which Jerusalem is the metropolis, is sunk in misery, driven with tempest like chaff of the threshing-floor (Hos 13:3), without comfort; because till now it has waited in vain for any act of consolation on the part of God, and has been scorned rather than comforted by man (סערה is a part. <hi type="italic">kal</hi>, not <hi type="italic">pual</hi>; and נחמה   3rd pers. <hi type="italic">praet</hi>. like נעזבה, <reference osisRef="Isa.62.12">Isa 62:12</reference>, and רחמה, Hos 1:6; Hos 2:3). But this will be altered; Jerusalem will rise again from the dust, like a glorious building of God. Jerome makes the following apt remark on <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Isa.54.11">Isa 54:11</reference></hi>: “<hi type="italic">in stibio</hi>, i.e., in the likeness of an elegant woman, who paints her eyes with <hi type="italic">stibium</hi>; referring to the beauty of the city.” <hi type="italic">Pūkh</hi> is eye-black (<hi type="italic">kohl</hi>, cf., <hi type="italic">kâchal</hi>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.23.40">Eze 23:40</reference>), i.e., a sooty compound, the chief component of which was powdered antimony, or else manganese or lead, and with which oriental women coloured their eyebrows, and more particularly the eyelids both above and below the eyes, that the beauty of the latter might be all the more conspicuous (2Ki 9:30). The classic φῦκος, <hi type="italic">fucus</hi>, has a meaning foreign to the Hebrew word, viz., that of rouge for the cheeks. If, then, <hi type="italic">stibium</hi> (antimony), or any blackening collyrium generally, served the purpose of mortar in the rebuilding of Jerusalem, the stones of its walls (not its foundation-stones, אדניך, which is the reading adopted by Ewald, but, on the contrary, the visible stones of its towering walls) would look like the eyes of a woman shining forth from the black framework of their painted lids, i.e., they would stand out in splendour from their dark ground. The <hi type="italic">Beth</hi> in <hi type="italic">bassappı̄rı̄m</hi> indicates the means employed. Sapphires serve as foundation-stones, for the foundation of Jerusalem stands as immoveably firm as the covenant of God. The sapphire blue is the colour of the heaven, of revelation, and of the covenant. The <hi type="italic">shemâshōth</hi>, however, i.e., the minarets which stand out like rays of the sun, and also the gates, have a red appearance. Red is the colour of blood, and hence of life and of imperishableness; also the colour of fire and of lightning, and hence of wrath and victory. Jehovah makes the minarets of “ruby.” The Sept. and Jerome adopt the rendering <hi type="italic">iaspidem</hi> (a jasper); at any rate, כּדכד (which is the proper way of writing the word: Ewald, §48,<hi type="italic">c</hi>)<note placement="foot">The first כ is <hi type="italic">dagessatum</hi>, the second <hi type="italic">raphatum</hi>: see Norzi. The word forms one of the eighteen which have a <hi type="italic">dagesh</hi> after a word ending with a vowel sound (בלא מבטל בתר יה וא דגשין): see <hi type="italic">Masora Magna</hi> on <reference osisRef="Dan.5.11">Dan 5:11</reference>, and Heidenheim’s הטעמים משפטי, 41 <hi type="italic">a</hi>. The object is to secure greater euphony, as in ככרכמישׁ (הלא), <reference osisRef="Isa.10.9">Isa 10:9</reference>, which is one of the eighteen words.</note> is a red sparkling jewel (from <hi type="italic">kidkēd</hi>; cf., <hi type="italic">kı̄dōd</hi>, <hi type="italic">scintilla</hi>). The arches of the gates He forms of אקדּח אבני, stones of fiery splendour (from <hi type="italic">qâdach</hi>, to burn: hence <hi type="italic">qaddachath</hi>, πυρετός), that is to say, or carbuncle stones (from <hi type="italic">carbunculus</hi>, a small red-hot coal), like ruby, garnet, etc. Jerome has adopted the false rendering <hi type="italic">lapides sculptos</hi>, after Symm. λίθοι γλυφῆς (from קדח = קדד, <hi type="italic">findere</hi>?). The accusative of the predicate כדכד is interchanged with עקדח לבני, and then with לאבני־חפץ, to denote the <hi type="italic">materia ex qua</hi>. The whole territory (precinct) of Jerusalem is turned by Jehovah into precious stones, that is to say, it appears to be paved with such stones, just as in Tobit 13:17 the streets are said to be “paved with beryl, and carbuncle, and stones of Ophir,” i.e., to be covered with a mosaic formed of precious stones. It is upon the passage before us that Tobit 13:16, 17, and <reference osisRef="Rev.21.18-Rev.21.21">Rev 21:18-21</reference>, are founded. The motley colours of the precious stones, with which the new Jerusalem is adorned, are something more than a mere childish fancy. Whence, then, do the precious stones derive their charm? The ultimate ground of this charm is the fact, that in universal nature everything presses to the light, and that in the mineral world the jewels represent the highest stage of this ascending process. It is the self-unfolding process of the divine glory itself, which is reflected typologically in the several gradations of the manifold play of colours and the transparency of the precious stones. For this reason, the high priest wore a breastplate with twelve precious stones, upon which were the names of the twelve tribes of Israel; and for this same reason, the author of the Apocalypse carries out into detail in chapter 21 the picture of the new Jerusalem, which is here sketched by the prophet of the Old Testament (without distinguishing time from eternity), adding crystals and pearls to the precious stones which he there mentions one by one. How can all this be explained, except on the ground that even the mineral world reflects the glory of those eternal lights from which God is called the “Father of lights,” or except on the assumption that the saints in light will one day be able to translate these stony types into the words of God, out of which they have their being?
entries.8224564774952b63af070eec14906e0cceaa037d: <reference osisRef="Isa.54.13">Isa 54:13</reference> <div eID="gen13540" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13541" type="x-p"/> The outward glory of the city is only the manifestation, which strikes the senses, of the spiritual glory of the church dwelling therein. <hi type="italic">“And all thy children will be the learned of Jehovah; and great the peace of thy children.”</hi> We translate both halves of the v. as substantive clauses, although they might be accusatives of both the object and predicate, dependent upon שׂמתּי. ה למּוּדי are disciples of Jehovah, but, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.50.4">Isa 50:4</reference>, with the subordinate idea of both docility and learning. The children of Jerusalem will need no instruction from man, but carry within them the teaching of heaven, as those who are “taught of God” (διδακτοὶ Θεοῦ, Joh 6:45; θεοδίδακτοι, <reference osisRef="1Thess.4.9">1Th 4:9</reference>). Essentially the same promise is given in <reference osisRef="Joel.3.1-Joel.3.2">Joe 3:1-2</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Jer.31.34">Jer 31:34</reference>; and represented in 1Jo 2:20 (<hi type="italic">“Ye have the anointing of the Holy One, and know all things”</hi>) as already fulfilled. In the place of the former inward and outward distress, there has no entered <hi type="italic">shâlōm</hi>, perfect inward and outward peace, complete salvation, and blessedness as its result. רב is an adjective, for this form cannot be shown to have existed as a syncopated third pers. <hi type="italic">praet</hi>., like שׁח, חי (= חיי). The v. closes palindromically.
entries.6a13aa6a6214d0a0d7df382355ae2ba6439506a4: <reference osisRef="Isa.54.14-Isa.54.15">Isa 54:14-15</reference> <div eID="gen13541" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13542" type="x-p"/> In perfect keeping with this grace through righteousness, Jerusalem will then stand firm and impregnable. <hi type="italic">“Through righteousness wilt thou be fortified: be far from anxiety, for thou hast nothing to fear; and from terror, for it will not come near thee. Behold, men crowd together in crowds; my will is not there. Who crowd together against thee? - he shall fall by thee.”</hi> Both the thought and action of Jerusalem will be righteousness then, and it will thereby acquire strength; תּכּונני is a pausal future <hi type="italic">hithpalel</hi>, with the ת of the reflective opening syllable assimilated (Ges. §53, 2,<hi type="italic">b</hi>). With this reciprocal influence of its moral character and imparted glory, it can, and is to keep far away from all thought of oppression and terror; for, through divine grace and a corresponding divine nature, it has nothing to fear. הן (<hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Isa.54.15">Isa 54:15</reference></hi>), when pointing to any transaction as possible (as, for example, in <reference osisRef="Job.12.14">Job 12:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.23.8">Job 23:8</reference>), acquires almost the significance of a conditional particle (Ewald, §103,<hi type="italic">g</hi>). The equally hypothetical parallel clause is clothed in the form of an interrogative. For the verb <hi type="italic">gūr</hi>, the meaning “to gather together” (related to אגר), more especially to join together with hostile intention (cf., συνάγεσθαι, <reference osisRef="Rev.19.19">Rev 19:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.20.8">Rev 20:8</reference>), is sustained by <reference osisRef="Ps.56.7">Psa 56:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.59.4">Psa 59:4</reference>; and with גּרה, <hi type="italic">lacessere</hi>, it has nothing to do (Hitzig and Ewald). אתּך has the force of <hi type="italic">contra te</hi>, as in the case of verbs of combat. The first apodosis is this: “but it takes place entirely away from me,” i.e., without and against my will; מאותי = מאתּי (as in <reference osisRef="Isa.59.21">Isa 59:21</reference>), and אותם = אתּם, are no sure signs of a later usage; for this alternation of the two forms of את is met with as early as Jos 14:12. The second apodosis is, “he will fall upon (or against) thee,” or, as we should say, “founder,” or “be wrecked.” It is far more likely that this is the meaning of the words, than that they mean “he will fall to thy lot” (על נפל, like ל נפל elsewhere, to fall to a person); for the context here is a totally different one from <reference osisRef="Isa.45.14">Isa 45:14</reference>, and we look for nothing more than a declaration of the utter failure and ruin of the undertaking.
entries.ff6e4c08c489c949999d0a087e37b17f9e6a3003: <reference osisRef="Isa.54.16-Isa.54.17">Isa 54:16-17</reference> <div eID="gen13542" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13543" type="x-p"/> Jerusalem will be thus invincible, because Jehovah, the Almighty One, is its protector. <hi type="italic">“Behold, I have created the smith who bloweth the coal-fire, and brings to the light a weapon according to his trade; and I have created the destroyer to destroy. Every weapon formed against thee has no success, and every tongue that cometh before the judgment with thee thou wilt condemn. This the inheritance of the servants of Jehovah; and their righteousness from me, saith Jehovah.”</hi> If Jehovah has created the armourer, who forges a weapon למעסהוּ (i.e., according to his trade, or according to the thing he has to finish, whether an arrow, or a sword, or a spear; not “for his own use,” as Kimchi supposes), to be used in the hostile army against Jerusalem, He has also created a destroyer (לחבּל) to destroy. The very same creative might, to which the origin of the weapon is to be traced as its primary cause, has opposed to it beforehand a defender of Jerusalem. And as every hostile weapon fails, Jerusalem, in the consciousness of its divine right, will convict every accusing tongue as guilty and deserving of utter condemnation (הרשׁיע as in <reference osisRef="Isa.50.9">Isa 50:9</reference>, cf., <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.47">1Sa 14:47</reference>, where it denotes the punishment of the guilty). The epiphonem in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Isa.54.17">Isa 54:17</reference></hi>, with the retrospective זאת and the words “saith the Lord,” which confirm the certainty of the fulfilment, forms an unmistakeable close to the prophecy. This is the position in which Jehovah has placed His servants as heirs of the future salvation; and this the righteousness which they have received as His gift, and which makes them strong within and victorious without. The individual idea of the church, which we find elsewhere personified as “the servant of Jehovah,” equivalent to “the people in whose heart is my law” (<reference osisRef="Isa.51.7">Isa 51:7</reference>), or “my people that have sought me” (<reference osisRef="Isa.65.10">Isa 65:10</reference>), is here expanded into “the servants of Jehovah” (as in <reference osisRef="Isa.65.8-Isa.65.9">Isa 65:8-9</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Isa.59.21">Isa 59:21</reference> with <reference osisRef="Isa.51.16">Isa 51:16</reference>). But totally different colours are employed in <reference osisRef="Isa.52.13">Isa 52:13</reference> to <reference osisRef="Isa.53.1-Isa.53.12">Isa 53:1-12</reference> to depict the exaltation of the one “Servant of Jehovah,” from those used here to paint the glory of the church of the “servants of Jehovah,” a proof that the ideas do not cover one another. That which is the reward of suffering in the case of the former, is the experience of divine mercy in that of the latter: it becomes a partaker of the salvation purchased by the other. The one “Servant of Jehovah” is the heart of the church, in which the crisis which bursts forth into life is passing; the righteousness of the “servants of Jehovah” is the fruit of the sufferings of this one “Servant of Jehovah,” who is Himself צדיק and מצידק. He is the Mediator of all the salvation of the church. He is not only its “head,” but its “fulness” (πλήρωμα) also.  <chapter eID="Isa.54"/> <div eID="gen13543" type="x-p"/>

                     <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ch. 61. 4, 5, 6.</ns0:note> shall inherit the Gentiles <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Shall subdue the Gentile World to the Church, and to the Obedience of the Faith.</ns0:note>, and make the desolate cities <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">These Cities and Countries which in a spiritual sense were desolate and forsaken by God.</ns0:note> to be inha<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bited.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="4">4 Fear not, for thou shalt not be ashamed <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">For that Barrenness and Widow-hood, which once was the matter of thy grief and shame, because now thou shalt be deliver<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed from it, and God will own thee for his Wife, and beget Chil<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dren of thee; as it is explained in the following words.</ns0:note>: nei<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther be thou confounded, for thou shalt not be put to shame: for thou shalt forget the shame of thy <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ezek. 23. 8.</ns0:note> youth <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">It shall be forgotten both by thee and others: thou shalt not be upbraided with thy former barrenness in thy youthful state, nor consounded and tormented with the remembrance of it; both <ns0:hi>remembring</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>forgetting</ns0:hi> in Scripture use connote or comprehend those affections which naturally and usually follow upon them; so great shall be thy fertility and felicity, that it shall cause thee to forget thy for<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mer unfruitfulness and misery, as Men commonly do in like cases, as <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 41. 51. <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> 11. 16. <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 65. 16. <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 16. 21.</ns0:note>, and shalt not remember the reproach of thy widowhood <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">That time and state when thou wert like a Widow disconsolate and desolate, forsaken by her Husband, and having in a manner no Children; which was a great reproach, especially among the Jews.</ns0:note> any more.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="5">5 For thy maker <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">He who made thee out of nothing, and therefore can easily fulfil all these Promises, how unlikely soever they seem to be; and he who made thee a people, and, which is far more & better, his Peo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ple, & therefore will not easily nor utterly forsake thee.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> thine husband <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">He will own thee for his Spouse, and will do the part of an Husband to thee.</ns0:note>, (the <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Luk. 1. 32.</ns0:note> LORD of hosts <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Who hath the soveraign command of all Men and Creatures, and therefore can subdue the Gentiles to thee, and can make thee to encrease and multiply in so prodigious a measure, even in thine old age, notwithstanding thy barrenness in the days of thy youth, of which he speaketh in the foregoing verse.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> his name) and thy redeemer the holy One of Israel, the God of the whole earth <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">The God and Fa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther of all Nations, whereas formerly he was called only <ns0:hi>the God of Israel,</ns0:hi> and the Gentiles had no special Relation to him, nor Interest in his Covenant and Favour, as was observed <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 147. 19, 20. and elsewhere.</ns0:note> shall he be called.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="6">6 For the LORD hath called thee <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">To return and come again to him.</ns0:note> as a woman <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">When thou wast like a Woman forsaken. Or, as an Husband recalleth his Wife.</ns0:note> forsaken and grieved in spirit <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">For the loss of her Husbands Favour and Society, and for the reproach at<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tending upon it.</ns0:note>, and a wife of youth <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>and, as</ns0:hi> (which note of similitude is sup<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />plied here by the Seventy, and Chaldee Interpreters, and is easily understood out of the foregoing clause, in which it is expressed) <ns0:hi>a wife of youth, i. e.</ns0:hi> as readily and affectionately as an Husband recalleth his Wife which he married in her and his own youth, of whom see on <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 5. 18. whom though he might through a sudden and violent passion put away, yet he soon repents of it, and his Affecti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ons work towards her, and he invites her to return to him.</ns0:note>, when thou <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Jer. 30. 17.</ns0:note> wast refused <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">When thou wast in a desolate Estate, and hadst been for some time rejected by me, then I recalled thee. Or, <ns0:hi>although thou wast refused,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>dismissed,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>despised</ns0:hi> by me, and that justly, yet I had mercy upon thee, and freely offered Reconciliation to thee.</ns0:note>, saith thy God <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Who will again be, and still shew himself to be, thy God, and will renew his Covenant with thee.</ns0:note>. <ns0:note place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>u</ns0:hi> By her Husband, who hath given her a Bill of Divorce.</ns0:note>
                  </ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="7">7 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ps. 30. 5. Ch. 26. 20. 2 Cor. 4. 17.</ns0:note> For a small moment <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">For the space of some few years, as Seventy years in <ns0:hi>Babylon,</ns0:hi> and some such intervals, which may well be called a <ns0:hi>small moment</ns0:hi> in comparison of Gods <ns0:hi>everlasting Kindness</ns0:hi> mentioned in the next verse.</ns0:note> have I forsaken thee <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Withdrawn my favour and help from thee, and left thee in thine Enemies hands.</ns0:note>, but with great mercies <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Such as are most precious and sweet for quality, as is here said, and such as are of long continuance, as is said in the following verse.</ns0:note> will I gather thee <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">From all the places where thou art dispersed, from all the parts of the World.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="8">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:615" />8 In a little wrath I hid my face <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">I removed the means and pledges of my presence and kind<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness.</ns0:note> from thee, for a moment; but with everlasting kindness <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">With kindness to thee and thy seed through all succeed<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing Generations, here and unto all eternity.</ns0:note> will I have mercy on thee, saith the LORD thy redeemer.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="9">9 For this <ns0:hi>is as</ns0:hi> the waters of <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Gen. 8. 21. & 9. 11.</ns0:note> Noah unto me <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">This Covenant of Grace and Peace made with thee shall be as certain and perpetual as that which I made with <ns0:hi>Noah,</ns0:hi> that there should never be another flood of waters to drown the World<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> of which see <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 9. 11.</ns0:note>: for <ns0:hi>as</ns0:hi> I have sworn that the waters of Noah should no more go over the earth, so have I sworn that I would not be wroth with thee <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">To wit, so as I have been, or so as to forsake thee utterly.</ns0:note>, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ps. 9. 5.</ns0:note> nor rebuke thee.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="10">10 For <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ps. 46. 2. Mat. 5. 18.</ns0:note> the mountains shall depart, and the hills be removed <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Which hath been verified in some Mountains and Hills, that by Earth-quakes, or otherwise, have been removed from their places. But these kinds of absolute expressions are oft times com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />paratively understood, of which see on <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 51. 6. and so the sense is, The Mountains shall sooner depart from their places, than my kindness shall depart from thee. As when it is said absolutely, <ns0:hi>I desired Mercy and not Sacrifice,</ns0:hi> it is meant comparatively, I desired Mercy more than Sacrifice, as it is explained in the following clause.</ns0:note>, but my kindness shall not depart from thee, neither shall the covenant of my peace <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">That covenant whereby I have made Peace and Friend<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ship with thee, and have promised unto thee all manner of happi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> which frequently comes under the name of <ns0:hi>peace</ns0:hi> in Scripture. The sense of the place is, That God will not cast off his Christian Church, as he did cast off the Church of the Jews; and that the New Covenant is established upon better and surer Promises than the Old, as is observed <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 8. 6, 7, &c. and elsewhere.</ns0:note> be re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />moved, saith the LORD, that hath mercy on thee <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Who doth thus with thee not for thy own merits, but meerly for his own Grace and Mercy.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="11">11 Oh thou afflicted, tossed with tempests, <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> not comforted <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Oh thou my poor Church, who hast frequently been, and wilt again and again be in a most afflicted and comfortless conditi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on for a time; be not discouraged thereby.</ns0:note>, behold, I will lay thy stones with <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 Chr. 29. 2. Rev. 21. 19.</ns0:note> fair colours, and lay thy foundations with saphires <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">I will make thee ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ceeding beautiful and glorious. Which yet is not to be under<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stood of outward Pomp and worldly Glory, as is evident from ma<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ny places of Scripture, which assure us that Christs Kingdom is of another nature, and that the external condition of Gods Church is, and for the most part will be, mean and calamitous in this World, but of a spiritual Beauty and Glory consisting in the plentiful effu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sion of excellent Gifts, and Graces, and Comforts: although these shall be followed with eternal Glory in Heaven. See the like description of the Churches Glory, <ns0:hi>Rev.</ns0:hi> 21. 11, &c.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="12">12 And I will make thy windows of agates <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">One kind of which stones was transparent like glass, as <ns0:hi>Pliny</ns0:hi> writes in his natural History, <ns0:hi>b.</ns0:hi> 37. <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 10. But some render this word, <ns0:hi>crystal,</ns0:hi> and the Seventy, and some other of the ancients, translate it <ns0:hi>jasper.</ns0:hi> But the proper signification of the Hebrew names of precious stones is unknown to the Jews themselves, as hath been noted before. It may suffice us to know that this was some very clear, and transparent, and precious stone.</ns0:note>, and thy gates of carbuncles, and all thy borders <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">The utmost parts or Walls. The Church is here evidently compared to a Building, whose <ns0:hi>Foundation, Pavement, Gates, and Windows,</ns0:hi> were named before.</ns0:note> of plea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sant stones.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="13">13 And all thy children <ns0:hi>shall be</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ch. 11. 9. Jer. 31. 34. Joh. 6. 45. 1 Cor. 2. 16. 1 Thes. 4. 9. 1 Joh. 2. 20.</ns0:note> taught of the LORD <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Not only outwardly by his word, which was made known to all the Jews under the Old Testament, but inwardly by his Spirit, which is poured forth under the New Testament, both upon a far greater number of persons, and in a far higher measure, and with much more efficacy and success than it was under the Old.</ns0:note>, and great <ns0:hi>shall be</ns0:hi> the peace <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">1. In<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ward Peace of Mind or Conscience arising from the clear discove<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ries of Gods Love and Reconciliation to us, and wrought by the spirit of adoption which is more abundantly given to Believers un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />der the Gospel, whereas the spirit of bondage was more common and prevalent under the Law. 2. Outward Peace, Safety, and Hap<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />piness, which is more fully promised in the following verses, and which God, when he sees fit will confer upon his Church.</ns0:note> of thy chil<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dren.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="14">14 In righteousness <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Either 1. As the means of thy Establishment. This Kingdom shall not be set up, and settled by fraud or Tyran<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ny, as other Kingdoms frequently are, but by Justice: Or rather 2. As the effect of the establishment. Thine affairs shall be managed with Righteousness, which is the Glory and Felicity of any society, and not with oppression, as it follows. Justice shall be freely and impartially executed.</ns0:note> shalt thou be established: thou shalt be far from oppression <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Either by thine own Governours, or by forreign Powers.</ns0:note>
                     <ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> for thou shalt not fear <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Thou shalt neither have any just cause of fear, nor be given up to the torment of fear without cause.</ns0:note>, and from terrour, for it shall not come near thee.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="15">15 Behold they shall surely gather together <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">It is true, there will not want some that shall combine and make an attempt against thee.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>but</ns0:hi> not by me <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">As they do this without any such commission from me, as <ns0:hi>Sennacherib</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Nebuchadnezzar</ns0:hi> had, <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 10. 6, 7. <ns0:hi>Ier.</ns0:hi> 25. 9. so they shall not have my help in it, without which all their endeavours will be vain and unsuccessful.</ns0:note>: whosoever shall gather together <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">To battle, as is manifest from the following words, of which kind of gathering this word is used <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 140. 2. and elsewhere.</ns0:note> against thee <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Heb. <ns0:hi>with thee.</ns0:hi> But <ns0:hi>to fight with a man</ns0:hi> is all one with <ns0:hi>fighting against him.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>, shall fall for thy sake <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">For that Respect and Love which I bear to thee. Or, <ns0:hi>before thee,</ns0:hi> as this particle is sometimes used, so as thine Eyes shall behold it.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="16">16 Behold, I have created the smith that bloweth the coals in the fire, and that bringeth forth an instru<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment for his work, and I have created the waster <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Both the Smith that maketh all warlike Instruments, and the Souldier that useth them, are my Creatures, and totally at my Com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mand, and therefore they cannot hurt you without my leave.</ns0:note> to destroy <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">To destroy only whom and when I please.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="17">17 No weapon that is formed against thee<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> shall prosper <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">And as they cannot do any thing against thee without my leave, so I assure thee I will not suffer them to do it: and if any Smith shall make any weapons to be employed against thee, he shall not succeed in it.</ns0:note>, and every tongue <ns0:hi>that</ns0:hi> shall rise against thee in judgment, thou shalt condemn <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">And I will deliver thee not only from the fury of War, but also from the strife of Tongues, from all the threatnings and boasts, and reproaches of thine Enemies, and from all the claims and pretences which they have of any right and power over thee. So thine Enemies shall neither prevail against thee by violence, nor by pretences of Justice.</ns0:note>. This <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> the heri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tage <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">This blessed condition described in this Chapter, is the portion allotted to them by me.</ns0:note> of the servants of the LORD, and their righte<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ousness <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Either 1. The Reward or Fruit of their Righteous<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness, as <ns0:hi>Righteousness</ns0:hi> is used <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 112. 3, 9. Or 2. Their Right or the righteous Administration of all their concerns where<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />by they are preserved from all manner of oppressions, as <ns0:hi>Righteous<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness</ns0:hi> was used <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 14.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> of me <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">I give it, and I will continue it to them, and who then can take it away from them.</ns0:note>, saith the LORD.</ns0:p>
